newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE-Leftist Lula back on Brazil election trail.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Leftist Lula back on Brazil election trail.

text.p: Twenty years ago, a gruff, unschooled trade unionist preaching class revolution took Brazilian politics by storm as he led crippling strikes against the country's military dictators.

Now, stung by two presidential election defeats but with his eye on a third attempt next year, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva still insists a strong dose of socialism is the only cure for Brazil's acute social problems.

"We've got 30 million people living in poverty and 20 percent of the population can't even read. Things have got to change," the former lathe operator, known throughout Brazil simply as Lula, told Reuters in an interview.
Brazil has changed greatly since opponents of the 1964-85 regime ran the gantlet of brutal police repression.

Pro-democracy activist Fernando Henrique Cardoso seemed to epitomize the change when he was elected president in 1994, but he snubbed the left by allying his social democrats with the conservative political elite that benefitted most from the dictatorship and dealing Lula a resounding election defeat.
"This government is only concerned with fiscal problems and reducing public debt. What social policies has it come up with in the last three years? None," Lula said.

Sadly for him and his Workers Party (PT), it is precisely Cardoso's fiscal achievements, exemplified by single-digit inflation, that makes him the firm favorite to win re-election. With many Brazilians marveling over their new-found spending power, the left has struggled to find a rallying cry. A national day of protest in July proved an embarrassing flop when only a few thousand marchers took to the streets.
BRAZILIANS TIRED OF AUSTERITY, LULA SAYS

Yet Lula insists Brazil is tired of paying the price of austere financial policies and is ready for the kind of shift to the left seen in recent elections around the world. "You can't stick to an economic plan forever, watching farms and factories go under and relying the whole time on foreign capital," he said. "One day, Brazil is going to snap."

Cardoso's critics warn that Brazil is at risk from the kind of devastating currency devaluation that brought Mexico to its knees in 1994. After the election of veteran leftist Cuauhtemoc Cardenas as Mexico City mayor in July, there have been fresh comparisons between Brazil and Mexico.
"Cardenas lost two elections for president and was written off as a no-hoper," Lula said. "He has shown that there is room for the left in Latin America."

But there is little chance the PT will follow the example of left-wing parties worldwide and moving to a voter-friendly political center. Renegotiation of Brazil's massive foreign debt, distribution of land for the landless, import tariffs to stave off foreign competiton -- all would be top of the agenda of any PT government, regardless of what investors may think.

"When a European says we're radical he's looking at us from a society which no longer needs ideas like these. Brazil is one of the world's top ten economies but still we're being compared with Botswana. Our poverty shouts out at us," Lula said.
BRAZIL RIPE FOR CHANGE?

To an outside observer, Brazil might appear ripe for change. Cardoso's success in curbing inflation has not been matched by a marked reduction in poverty or improved services. Clashes over land continue to claim lives and some police officers recently held violent protests over pay, forcing the president to send troops to several cities to keep order.

But Cardoso is still expected to cruise to a second term. Political analysts say the opposition has failed to find a credible alternative for an electorate that wants a fairer Brazil, but not if it means a return to economic chaos.
"The PT has wasted the last four years when they could have come up with a new message," said Franklin Martins, a political columnist with newspaper O Globo.

Rather than change policies, Brazil's left is pinning its hopes for the October 1998 elections on a change in tactics. In an unusual show of unity, half a dozen opposition parties say they will back Lula as a single left-wing candidate.
Even veteran populist Leonel Brizola, who once called Lula "a bearded toad," says he will bury his unsatisfied political ambitions to avoid a costly split in the left-wing vote.
Lula himself coyly declines to declare his candidacy officially but says "If I was the only candidate with a chance of beating (Cardoso) I would not run from my responsibilties."

But few doubt he is in pre-campaign mode. He is already preparing a rerun of a 1994 pre-election trek through Brazil's poorest corners to show the plight of its vast underclass. And it is a smiling, child-hugging Lula who features in the PT's prime-time television spots berating the government over its record on unemployment, health and education.
Next year, he believes, it could be third time charmed.
